Reading motivation is one instance of the broader challenge of sustaining intrinsic motivation for intellectually demanding self-directed learning across a lifetime.
**Connection to this report:** Provides the macro-level motivational architecture within which the specific reading motivation strategies of this report are embedded.
**Priority:** Critical
**Suggested report type:** Foundational Report
**Prerequisites:** [[Self-Determination-Theory]], [[Andragogy]], [[Personal-Knowledge-Management]]

Academic reading, as distinct from leisure or functional reading, involves texts that make systematic cognitive demands: abstract concepts with high element interactivity, unfamiliar domain vocabulary, complex argument structures requiring sustained working memory, and information densities that frequently exceed what can be processed in real-time. These properties create what [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] terms high [[Intrinsic-Cognitive-Load]] — load that is inherent to the material itself rather than to poor instructional design. The implication is significant: no amount of motivational scaffolding alone will sustain academic reading in the absence of the cognitive skills necessary to make engagement rewarding. Nor, conversely, will the most finely tuned cognitive strategies produce sustained academic reading in a learner who has no intrinsically motivating reason to persist.

wiki_links.section: 1.2 Why Academic Reading Is Structurally Motivationally Challenging
wiki_links.context_line: Academic reading is motivationally challenging for reasons that go beyond mere difficulty. Several structural features of academic texts directly undermine the conditions for need satisfaction identified by [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]]:

wiki_links.section: 1.2 Why Academic Reading Is Structurally Motivationally Challenging
wiki_links.context_line: **Competence threat:** Academic texts regularly produce comprehension failure, ambiguity, and confusion. For readers with a [[Fixed-Mindset]] orientation toward their reading ability, each instance of confusion is interpreted as evidence of incompetence rather than as a normal and productive stage of learning. The result is what Carol Dweck's research identifies as the helpless response pattern: withdrawal of effort, avoidance of challenge, and motivated dismissal of difficult material. [[Self-Efficacy]] — the reader's belief in their capacity to comprehend challenging texts — is among the strongest predictors of academic reading persistence across multiple meta-analyses.

wiki_links.section: 1.2 Why Academic Reading Is Structurally Motivationally Challenging
wiki_links.context_line: **Autonomy erosion:** Much academic reading is externally mandated — reading lists, coursework requirements, examination preparation. When the perceived locus of causality for reading is external (I am reading because I must), [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]] predicts a reduction in intrinsic motivation, particularly if the external requirement is experienced as controlling rather than informational. The experience of being required to read is not inherently demotivating — SDL frameworks document numerous conditions under which external requirements can be internalized and become autonomous — but the structural conditions of academic environments often work against this internalization.

wiki_links.section: 1.2 Why Academic Reading Is Structurally Motivationally Challenging
wiki_links.context_line: **Relatedness disconnection:** Academic texts are typically produced within epistemic communities that beginning readers have not yet joined. The discourse conventions, citation practices, implicit assumptions, and field-specific argument norms create a felt sense of alienation — reading that produces the unsettling experience of understanding individual sentences without understanding what is actually being argued, and why it matters. This disconnection undermines the [[Relatedness-Need]] dimension of need satisfaction, which in reading contexts manifests as a sense of genuine dialogue with the author's project.

wiki_links.section: 1.3 The Stakes: Why This Matters for Lifelong Learning
wiki_links.context_line: The consequences of failing to develop motivated academic reading capacity extend well beyond academic performance. [[Lifelong-learning]] as a genuine practice requires the ability to engage with the primary literature of new knowledge domains — not merely curated summaries or popular treatments. Readers who cannot sustain engagement with challenging texts are confined to the derivative and the simplified, which systematically limits their epistemic development. The [[Matthew-Effect]] in reading compounds this: early reading skill and motivation predict adult reading habits, which in turn determine knowledge accumulation trajectories. The rich get richer; the early disengaged remain cognitively hungry.

wiki_links.context_line: From the perspective of [[Personal-Knowledge-Management]], motivated academic reading is a foundational skill — the primary mechanism through which external knowledge becomes owned, elaborated, and appropriately connected to existing conceptual structures. A PKB system populated primarily with summaries and clippings represents extracted information; a PKB populated through deeply motivated engaged reading represents transformed knowledge. The contrast matters enormously for long-term intellectual development and creative synthesis.

wiki_links.section: 2.1 The Three-Level Architecture of Text Representation
wiki_links.context_line: Understanding why motivated academic reading requires sophisticated cognitive scaffolding begins with the cognitive science of text comprehension. Contemporary reading science, building on the foundational model developed by [[Walter-Kintsch]] and colleagues, identifies three hierarchically organized levels of text representation that competent readers construct simultaneously:

wiki_links.section: 2.1 The Three-Level Architecture of Text Representation
wiki_links.context_line: **The situation model level** represents an analog simulation of the state of affairs the text describes — a mental model of the domain being discussed, its entities, their relationships, and the causal and logical structure connecting them. The [[Situation-Models]] framework, developed by Kintsch and van Dijk, holds that genuine comprehension — as opposed to recognition or recall — requires successful situation model construction. A reader who has built a robust situation model can answer inference questions never explicitly posed by the text, can detect inconsistencies between what the text claims and what they know from other sources, and can transfer knowledge from the text to novel problems.

wiki_links.section: 2.2 The Role of Prior Knowledge and Schema in Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: The most robust predictor of situation model quality is not general reading skill but domain-specific [[Prior-Knowledge]]. This finding, well-established in the reading research literature (Alexander, Kulikowich & Schulze, 1994; McNamara et al., 1996), has profound implications for how motivation and comprehension interact. Prior knowledge enables readers to generate elaborative inferences that bridge explicit text statements to background understanding, building situation models that are richer and more durable than the textbase alone could support.

wiki_links.section: 2.2 The Role of Prior Knowledge and Schema in Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: [[Schema-Theory]] explains this mechanism: existing [[Schema|schemata]] provide organizational frameworks that facilitate encoding of new information, flag anomalies and violations that would otherwise pass unnoticed, and guide inference generation during comprehension. A reader with a rich crystallized schema for evolutionary biology reads a paper on niche construction very differently than a reader encountering the concepts for the first time — not merely because they understand more vocabulary, but because the conceptual architecture available to them transforms what inferential connections are available and which are automatic versus effortful.

Readers who read extensively in a domain build larger and better-organized schemata, which makes future reading in that domain more cognitively rewarding (more inferential payoff per unit attention), which reinforces reading motivation. Conversely, readers with thin domain knowledge experience academic reading as effortful symbol manipulation with little emergent comprehension, which is motivationally aversive and drives withdrawal. This is the cognitive face of the [[Matthew-Effect]] in academic reading.

wiki_links.section: 2.2 The Role of Prior Knowledge and Schema in Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: > There is a bootstrapping problem at the heart of motivated academic reading development that most intervention approaches fail to acknowledge explicitly. Domain knowledge facilitates motivated reading, and motivated reading builds domain knowledge — but how does one enter the virtuous cycle when starting from low prior knowledge? The answer, supported by research on [[Advance-Organizers]] and [[Conceptual-Change-Theory]], is that the entry point requires deliberate structural scaffolding: pre-reading activities that build surface-level familiarity with key concepts (not deep understanding — just enough schema to enable basic inference generation), combined with explicit acknowledgment that initial confusion is normative and expected. The motivational function of advance organizers is as much about reducing competence threat as it is about facilitating encoding.

wiki_links.section: 2.3 Working Memory Constraints and Cognitive Load in Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: [[Working-Memory-in-Reading]] plays a central mediating role between reading skill and comprehension quality. Academic texts frequently impose high [[Intrinsic-Cognitive-Load]] through: multi-clause sentence structures that require holding earlier clauses active while parsing later ones; dense referential chains (pronouns, nominalizations) that require active tracking; abstract concepts with many interacting elements; and arguments that unfold across multiple paragraphs, requiring long-range textual integration.

wiki_links.section: 2.3 Working Memory Constraints and Cognitive Load in Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] predicts that when total cognitive load (intrinsic + extraneous) exceeds working memory capacity, processing quality degrades predictably in the direction of shallower representations. Readers encountering high-load academic texts in challenging conditions (fatigue, distraction, time pressure, insufficient prior knowledge) will default to surface processing — reading for recognition rather than comprehension — regardless of their motivational orientation. This creates an important practical implication: motivation alone cannot override working memory constraints. Strategy instruction that reduces extraneous load (clear note structures, spaced reading sessions, vocabulary pre-loading) creates cognitive space for motivated deep processing to occur.

wiki_links.section: 2.4 Reading Fluency as the Foundation of Comprehension
wiki_links.context_line: At the most foundational level, academic reading competence depends upon [[Reading-Fluency]] — the automaticity and accuracy of word recognition, syntactic parsing, and lower-order decoding processes. The [[Simple-View-of-Reading]] framework (Gough & Tunmer, 1986) formulates reading comprehension as the product of decoding skill and linguistic comprehension: RC = D × LC. This multiplicative relationship means that deficiencies in either component cannot be compensated by strength in the other.

wiki_links.section: 2.4 Reading Fluency as the Foundation of Comprehension
wiki_links.context_line: [[Verbal-Efficiency-Theory]] (Perfetti, 1985) extends this analysis: reading fluency frees working memory resources that can then be allocated to higher-order comprehension processes. A reader who must consciously allocate resources to word recognition has fewer resources available for inference generation and situation model construction. The relationship between fluency and comprehension is therefore not merely correlational but mechanistically causal: fluency development is a prerequisite for the cognitive conditions under which motivated deep reading becomes possible. This is why the strategy hierarchy developed in Section 6 begins with fluency interventions rather than higher-order comprehension or motivational techniques.

wiki_links.section: 3.1 Reading Motivation as a Multidimensional Construct
wiki_links.context_line: Reading motivation is not a single psychological variable but a cluster of interrelated constructs that predict different aspects of reading behavior. The field has progressively moved from treating reading motivation as a unitary disposition (high vs. low motivation) toward recognizing that its multidimensional nature demands disaggregated analysis. Wigfield and Guthrie's seminal work on the [[Motivated-Strategies-for-Learning-Questionnaire|Motivation for Reading Questionnaire]] (1997) identified eleven distinct motivation dimensions — including reading self-efficacy, value for reading, reading curiosity, social motivations, reading challenge, and compliance — each of which independently predicts different reading behaviors and outcomes.

wiki_links.section: 3.2 Interest Theory and Its Reading Applications
wiki_links.context_line: The study of [[interest|interest]] as a motivational state provides one of the most actionable frameworks for understanding reading motivation. Hidi and Renninger's four-phase model of interest development distinguishes between situational interest (triggered by features of a text or context) and individual interest (a stable personal orientation toward a topic), with each having triggered and maintained sub-phases. This developmental model has significant implications for how reading experiences should be sequenced.

wiki_links.section: 3.3 Expectancy-Value Theory and the Reading Decision
wiki_links.context_line: [[Expectancy-Value-Theory]] (Eccles et al., 1983; Wigfield & Eccles, 2000) provides a complementary framework for understanding reading motivation at the level of specific task engagement decisions. The model proposes that the motivation to engage in a specific reading task is jointly determined by the expectancy of success (Can I understand this?) and the subjective value of the task (Is understanding this worth my time and effort?).

wiki_links.section: 3.4 The Concept of Reading Habit: Behavioral Regularity and Motivational Dependence
wiki_links.context_line: One of the most practically significant distinctions in reading motivation research concerns the difference between motivationally dependent reading behavior (reading that occurs only when motivation is high) and reading as a [[Habit-Formation|structured habit]] that is initiated and maintained partly independently of motivational state. The habit formation literature, particularly James Clear's synthesis of Duhigg and the behavioral science literature on automaticity, distinguishes between actions controlled by conscious motivational deliberation and actions controlled by contextual cues and established behavioral routines.

wiki_links.section: 4.2 The Three Needs Applied to Reading Environments
wiki_links.context_line: **Autonomy need satisfaction in reading:** Autonomy in academic reading contexts involves the experience of volition and self-endorsement in reading choices and methods. Autonomy is supported when readers have meaningful choice over *what* they read within a domain (even within structured curricula, choice among alternative texts satisfies autonomy), *when* they read (scheduling agency rather than external time imposition), *how* they read (choice of annotation style, reading pace, notetaking approach), and *why* — when the purpose of reading is genuinely self-endorsed rather than experienced as imposed. [[Autonomy-Support]] in reading environments experimentally increases intrinsic motivation, depth of processing, and transfer of learning relative to controlling environments, even holding text and instruction constant.

wiki_links.section: 4.2 The Three Needs Applied to Reading Environments
wiki_links.context_line: **Competence need satisfaction in reading:** Competence satisfaction in reading requires that readers experience themselves as effective comprehenders — not necessarily fluent or effortless, but genuinely growing in understanding capacity. This requires feedback mechanisms that provide accurate information about comprehension rather than simply performance (the question "Did you understand this section?" is more competence-satisfying than "What grade did you get on the reading quiz?"). Optimally challenging texts — those in the reader's [[Zone-of-Proximal-Development|zone of proximal development]] — satisfy the competence need by matching difficulty to current skill plus supportive scaffolding. Texts dramatically below or above current skill undermine competence satisfaction in different ways.

wiki_links.section: 4.2 The Three Needs Applied to Reading Environments
wiki_links.context_line: **Relatedness need satisfaction in reading:** Relatedness satisfaction in reading manifests as a sense of connection to the author's intellectual project, to a community of inquiry that shares genuine interest in the questions the text addresses, or to historical figures and traditions whose thinking the text represents. This is why seminar discussions, study groups, and writing communities can powerfully support academic reading motivation even when the cognitive work is solitary: they provide the social embedding that makes reading feel contributory rather than isolated. [[Psychological-Safety-in-Learning-Environments]] is a prerequisite for this kind of relatedness satisfaction — readers must feel that their confusions and misinterpretations can be voiced without shame.

Readers who begin their academic reading careers in a state of [[External-Regulation]] (I read only when directly required and monitored) can, under appropriate conditions, develop increasingly autonomous regulatory structures: [[Identified-Regulation]] (I read this because I genuinely care about the knowledge), and ultimately [[Integrated-Regulation]] (reading-for-understanding is a core expression of who I am as a person committed to intellectual growth).

The practical implication is that reading curriculum designers and self-directed learners have genuine agency over their internalization trajectories through deliberate environmental design.

wiki_links.section: 4.4 Goal Content Theory and Reading Purposes
wiki_links.context_line: [[Goal-Contents-Theory]] (Kasser & Ryan, 1996), one of SDT's mini-theories, distinguishes between intrinsic goal content (growth, meaning, contribution, connection) and extrinsic goal content (wealth, fame, image, power). While GCT was originally developed in the context of life aspirations rather than academic motivation, its logic applies directly to reading purposes. Readers who frame their academic reading in terms of intrinsic goal content — reading to understand something genuinely interesting, to develop expertise in service of meaningful contributions, to connect with the intellectual heritage of a discipline — demonstrate higher engagement, deeper processing, and greater reading persistence under difficulty compared to readers who frame reading in terms of extrinsic goal content — reading to perform well on assessments, to impress peers, or to fulfill external requirements.

wiki_links.section: 4.4 Goal Content Theory and Reading Purposes
wiki_links.context_line: > Academic reading is persistently threatened by what might be called the extrinsic goal framing trap: the institutional and social ecology of academic settings continuously primes extrinsic goal content (grades, credentials, performance demonstrations), and learners spontaneously adopt these frames even for content they would otherwise find intrinsically interesting. The corrosive effect is not merely motivational but cognitive: [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]] predicts that extrinsic goal framing produces surface-level processing strategies (what do I need to know to pass the test?) at the expense of deep processing strategies (what does this actually mean and how does it connect to what I know?). Learners who wish to maintain motivated deep reading in institutional contexts must actively and deliberately maintain intrinsic goal frames against the constant pressure of extrinsic environmental cues.

This distinction predicts qualitatively different patterns of reading behavior.

wiki_links.section: 5.2 The 2×2 Achievement Goal Framework and Reading Quality
wiki_links.context_line: Elliot and McGregor's 2×2 [[Achievement-Goal]] framework (2001) refines the mastery-performance distinction by crossing it with an approach-avoidance dimension, yielding four goal types with different reading implications:

wiki_links.section: 5.3 Entity vs. Incremental Theories of Reading Ability
wiki_links.context_line: [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]] is closely connected to Carol Dweck's framework of implicit theories of ability. Readers who hold an entity theory of reading ability (the belief that reading skill is a fixed, largely innate capacity) demonstrate characteristic responses to reading difficulty: they interpret comprehension failures as diagnostic of their fixed, limited reading ability; they withdraw effort under difficulty (since effort cannot overcome fixed limitations); and they disengage from challenging texts to preserve their ability self-concept.

wiki_links.section: 5.3 Entity vs. Incremental Theories of Reading Ability
wiki_links.context_line: Readers who hold an incremental theory of reading ability (the belief that reading skill is malleable and developed through effort and strategy) respond to difficulty by increasing strategic effort, seeking out challenge, and treating comprehension failures as informative feedback about what strategies need adjustment. The practical implication directly mirrors [[Growth-Mindset]] interventions in other domains: belief change regarding the malleability of reading ability is a legitimate and effective reading motivation intervention target.

**Fluency practice for academic texts:** While college-level readers are typically beyond the initial stages of decoding acquisition, academic fluency at the lexical, syntactic, and propositional levels often requires deliberate development. [[Deliberate-Practice]] applied to reading fluency involves timed re-reading of discipline-specific texts to build sublexical automaticity for domain vocabulary and syntactic patterns, reducing the processing resources required for lower-order comprehension and freeing cognitive capacity for situation model construction. This is particularly important in highly technical fields (philosophy, law, economics) where domain discourse has characteristic syntactic structures that require extended exposure to become fluent.

**Strategic text selection and sequencing:** A critical Tier 1 strategy is the management of text difficulty relative to current skill. The [[Desirable-Difficulties]] framework (Bjork, 1994) clarifies that some difficulty is beneficial for learning (interleaving, spacing, testing) while other difficulty is merely impeding (text that exceeds current vocabulary or prior knowledge by too much to enable productive inference). Selecting texts that are at the edge of current comprehension but not dramatically beyond it — texts where the reader can understand approximately 70-80% and must actively work to reconstruct the remaining 20-30% — maximizes both learning and motivational engagement. A reading curriculum that does not systematically manage difficulty progression implicitly asks readers to engage with texts before the cognitive prerequisites are in place.

**Elaborative interrogation:** [[Elaborative-Interrogation]] is a strategy involving the generation of explanatory "why" and "how" questions while reading, which prompts elaborated understanding and connects new information to prior knowledge networks. The mechanism is straightforward: answering self-generated why questions requires active construction of causal relationships that the text may not have stated explicitly, essentially forcing situation model construction. The effect size literature on elaborative interrogation (Pressley et al., 1992) consistently shows significant comprehension and retention benefits relative to restating or summarizing without elaboration.

**Self-explanation:** [[self-explanation]] (Chi et al., 1994) involves generating explanatory verbalizations of text content during reading — explaining to oneself what each section means, how it relates to preceding content, and what gaps remain in understanding. Self-explanation is one of the most robustly effective learning strategies in the research literature, with effects on comprehension quality, inference generation, and transfer of learning that exceed most other single strategies. Its mechanism overlaps with elaborative interrogation but extends to include explicit monitoring of comprehension: the self-explanation process surfaces the distinction between text understanding and situation model construction because it requires the reader to say in their own words what is understood, revealing gaps that re-reading without self-explanation would not detect.

**The KWL strategy and pre-questioning:** The [[KWL-Strategy]] (Ogle, 1986) — What do I Know? What do I Want to know? What did I Learn? — operationalizes the advance organizer principle through explicit pre-reading schema activation and curiosity generation. The Want-to-Know component is particularly motivationally significant: generating genuine questions before reading creates a cognitive and motivational orientation of inquiry rather than reception — the reader enters the text looking for answers to self-generated questions, which is functionally equivalent to creating situational interest in the content. Pre-questioning generalizes this principle beyond the three-column structure: generating several genuine questions about a text's domain before reading consistently improves both comprehension and motivation in comparison conditions.

**Annotation and active reading techniques:** The practice of systematic annotation during reading — marginalia, question marks, asterisks for key claims, explicit notation of confusions, underlines with brief explanatory notes — serves multiple functions simultaneously: it reduces cognitive load by externalizing textual navigation, it creates a visible record of comprehension monitoring (distinguishing passages where understanding is confident from those where it is uncertain), and it produces an output that has value for subsequent review and knowledge integration. [[Active-Note-Making]] during reading also serves the self-explanation function when annotations include explanatory paraphrases rather than mere highlighting.

**Retrieval practice integration:** [[Retrieval-Practice]] — the active retrieval of learned material from memory rather than passive re-exposure — is among the most robust findings in memory and learning science (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006). Applied to academic reading, retrieval practice means closing the text after a reading segment and actively reconstructing the main points and arguments from memory before checking accuracy against the text. This practice directly addresses the fluency illusion (the subjective familiarity that makes re-reading feel effective without producing durable memory) by forcing explicit retrieval that surfaces genuine memory failures. The testing effect also applies to reading comprehension: retrieving information from an academic text strengthens memory for that text significantly more than equivalent time re-reading it.

**[[Spaced-Repetition]] of reading notes:** Spacing and interleaving are canonical [[Desirable-Difficulties]] that increase long-term retention relative to massed practice. Applying spaced repetition to the material from academic reading — through spaced review of reading notes, summary cards, or structured flashcard systems — converts ephemeral textbase processing into durable situation model components that extend the effective life of each reading session many-fold. The combination of initial deep processing during reading (via self-explanation and elaborative interrogation) with subsequent spaced retrieval practice creates the optimal conditions for durable knowledge acquisition from academic texts.

wiki_links.section: 7.1 The Metacognitive Architecture of Expert Reading
wiki_links.context_line: [[Metacognition]] — cognition about one's own cognition — is among the most consistent predictor variables distinguishing skilled from less-skilled academic readers. Expert readers maintain an active, parallel monitoring process during reading that tracks comprehension quality in real time, detects failures, and initiates adaptive responses. Less-skilled readers often proceed through texts without adequate awareness that they have not understood what they have read — a deficit that is both cognitive and motivational: it prevents strategic adaptation and it produces false impressions of comprehension that deprive the reader of the competence experiences that genuine understanding generates.

wiki_links.section: Far Transfer: Applying These Insights Beyond Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: The principles underlying motivated academic reading are not specific to the textual medium or the academic context. The frameworks and mechanisms analyzed in this report have structural parallels across domains that reward sustained, cognitively demanding engagement — domains where [[Transfer-of-Learning]] through structural mapping provides genuine insight.

wiki_links.section: Far Transfer: Applying These Insights Beyond Academic Reading
wiki_links.context_line: > **Structural principle:** The four-system model (cognitive capacity, strategy, motivation, metacognition) applies to any cognitively demanding skill that requires sustained deliberate practice to develop. [[Deliberate-Practice]] theory (Ericsson) and [[Deep-Work]] (Newport) converge on the same architectural insight: sustained high-quality cognitive work requires threshold cognitive capacity, deliberate strategy, autonomous motivation, and ongoing self-monitoring. The vicious cycle analysis (poor capacity → poor experience → poor motivation → avoidance → continued poor capacity) is domain-general.

wiki_links.context_line: > **Application:** A learner who reads academic texts without an integrated PKM workflow operates at the textbase level — they may comprehend the text during reading, but without the external knowledge architecture, the situation model decays. PKM practice extends the situation model by externalizing it in a persistent, searchable, and interconnectable structure. The motivation-building strategies for academic reading — interest sequencing, reading identity development, autonomy-supportive practice design — apply equally to PKM practice and other [[Lifelong-Learning]] frameworks.

DIAGNOSTIC DECISION TREE

Reader cannot sustain engagement?
├─ Has good motivation but poor comprehension?
│   └─► INTERVENE AT TIER 2
│
├─ Has good comprehension but loses motivation over time?
│   └─► INTERVENE AT TIER 3
│

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          THREE LEVELS OF TEXT REPRESENTATION (Kintsch & van Dijk)        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TEXT COMPREHENSION
│
├── Level 1: SURFACE CODE
│   │
│   ├── Definition: verbatim linguistic content, exact words & syntax
│   ├── Duration: highly transient — lost within seconds/minutes
│   ├── Use: minimal academic utility on its own
│   └── Target of: rote memorization, verbatim copying
│
├── Level 2: TEXTBASE
│   │
│   ├── Definition: propositional content — what the text stated
│   ├── Duration: moderate — supports recall and paraphrase
│   ├── Use: adequate for factual recall; insufficient for transfer
│   └── Target of: most common study strategies
│           ├── note-taking (without elaboration)
│           ├── underlining / highlighting
│           └── summary writing without self-explanation
│
└── Level 3: SITUATION MODEL  ◄──── TARGET FOR ACADEMIC READING
    │
    ├── Definition: analog mental model of the world the text describes
    │   (entities, causal relationships, logical structure)
    ├── Duration: durable — enables transfer and inference
    ├── Use: genuine comprehension, novel problem transfer, PKM integration
    └── Target of: evidence-based Tier 2 strategies
            ├── self-explanation ("what does this mean in my words?")
            ├── elaborative interrogation ("why is this true?")
            ├── retrieval practice (forces model testing)
            └── annotation with explanatory paraphrases

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE GAP: Most academic readers target Level 2.
         Most academic purposes require Level 3.
         The strategies to reach Level 3 require motivated effort.

Phase 1 │ Choose high situational-interest texts on target topic

        │ Avoid dense/abstract materials prematurely
        │ Create positive first encounters with domain ideas

        │ Sequence texts with gradually increasing difficulty

        │ Encourage self-generated questions as reading driver

TOP 5 TAKEAWAYS:

1. Cognitive competence and reading motivation are STRUCTURALLY
   INTERDEPENDENT — one cannot be fixed in isolation from the other.

2. Most study strategies target the TEXTBASE level (recall & paraphrase).
   Academic purposes require SITUATION MODEL construction (transfer
   & genuine understanding). Self-explanation and retrieval practice
   are the highest-evidence bridges between these levels.

3. The three-tier strategy hierarchy is ARCHITECTURAL, not a priority
   ranking. Diagnose the lowest failing tier; intervene there first.

4. Goal orientation (mastery vs. performance-avoidance) is a DIAGNOSTIC
   before any strategy prescription. The same strategy works
   very differently depending on the reader's goal orientation.

5. Metacognitive monitoring during reading — explicitly tracking whether
   a situation model is forming — is the single highest-leverage
   metacognitive skill for academic readers, and the one most routinely
   neglected under cognitive load.
